messages.subject: Using plyr with boot
parts:
Hi Plyrs: Not sure if this can be done at all, but I am sure I'm not
doing it right!

df <- data.frame(res = rnorm(30),
gen = sample(c("A", "B"), 30, replace = T),
trt = sample(c("H", "L"), 30, replace = T))

mm <- function(d, i) median(d[i])

boot1 <-boot(df$res, mm, R = 1000)
# works fine, returns class "boot" which is a list

# Here is conceptually what I'd like to do:
# break out the df by its factor combinations, then
# bootstrap the resulting pieces & return the result
# I think the return value will be a list of lists(?)

boot2 <- dlply(.data = df, .variables = ~ gen + trt)
# works as expected, creates the desired list elements,
# but need access to e.g. boot2$A.H$res for the bootstrap

boot3 <- dlply(.data = df, .variables = ~ gen + trt, .fun = boot, data
= df$res, statistic = mm, R = 1000)

# several complaints from boot indicating it is
# not getting the right data type

# I think the problem is in the data specification, but
# maybe it can be addressed in the function mm?
# or, I've screwed up the call to boot?

Thanks, Bryan
Prof. of Chemistry & Biochemistry
DePauw University, Greencastle IN USA

parts:
Hi Bryan:

This appears to work for me:

df <- data.frame(res = rnorm(30),
       gen = sample(c("A", "B"), 30, replace = T),
       trt = sample(c("H", "L"), 30, replace = T))

boot(df$res, mm, R = 1000)
    }
boot3 <- dlply(.data = df, .variables = ~ gen + trt, .fun = boot0)

> class(boot3)
[1] "list"
> length(boot3)
[1] 4
> str(boot3[[1]])
List of 11
 $ t0       : num 0.295
 $ t        : num [1:1000, 1] 0.295 0.366 0.481 0.662 0.224 ...
 $ R        : num 1000
 $ data     : num [1:6] 0.366 0.224 0.597 -1.671 -1.164 ...
 $ seed     : int [1:626] 403 314 330191731 -754429888 2121303146 1902110828 1804437836 -1743472814 -27742768 -652603360 ...
 $ statistic:function (d, i) 
  ..- attr(*, "source")= chr "function(d, i) median(d[i])"
 $ sim      : chr "ordinary"
 $ call     : language boot(data = df$res, statistic = mm, R = 1000)
 $ stype    : chr "i"
 $ strata   : num [1:6] 1 1 1 1 1 1
 $ weights  : num [1:6] 0.167 0.167 0.167 0.167 0.167 ...
 - attr(*, "class")= chr "boot"

You should be able to use do.call() or plyr to extract pieces as necessary.

BTW, the code for boot2 was very useful - it's nice to know how to split into a list by more than one factor :)

HTH,
Dennis

PS: I had to try to plot histograms of the bootstrap medians by group, so this is what I cobbled up.

f <- function(l) unlist(l[2])   # extracts bootstrap medians into a numeric vector
 tst <- ldply(boot3, f)
dim(tst)      # a 4 x 1002 data frame - first two columns are the factors :)
[1]    4 1002
# Melt this puppy...
tst2 <- melt(tst, id = c('gen', 'trt'))
# Plot
g <- ggplot(tst2, aes(x = value, y = ..density..))
g + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) + facet_grid(gen ~ trt)

messages.subject: Re: Using plyr with boot
parts:
Well, as usual Dennis, you have helped me reconceptualize the problem entirely!

Your example function (boot0) was very different than any way I was thinking about solving the problem.   I played with it for a while, and looked at your histogram plot and asked myself what did I really want out of my analysis?  I was really after the bootstrap median and ci’s.  At some point, I remembered that ggplot2 had some boot strapping built in to stat_summary.  I studied that, wrote something overly complicated using the functions from Hmisc, then boiled it down to this very lean code with the ggplot2 built-ins:

df <- data.frame(res = rnorm(30),
    gen = sample(c("A", "B"), 30, replace = T),
    trt = sample(c("H", "L"), 30, replace = T))

#### Really clean code, includes original data points as “freckles”

jit <- position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.0)
p <- ggplot(data = df, aes(y = res, x = gen, color = gen))
p <- p + layer(geom = "jitter", position = jit, color = "black", size = 1)
p <- p + facet_grid(.~trt) + ylab("Bootstrap Mean +/- CI") + xlab("")
p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "median_hilow")
print(p)    

The final answer is so compact and of course it shows how Hadley anticipated guys like me.  I’m a little embarassed – I didn’t mean to illustrate to the whole group the random-walk of my critical thinking skills!  When I see this evolution of thought-process in my students and the light “goes on”, I’m always pleased when they “get it”, but in myself...

A big thanks to Dennis, and a nod to the prescient Hadley!

Bryan
*************
Bryan Hanson
Professor of Chemistry & Biochemistry
DePauw University, Greencastle IN USA
